evidence_quotes.quote: The results are presented according to three case studies conducted in Kenya and two in Ghana (Table 1). Case studies in both countries were performed in areas with medium to high population density, including low and middle income families, which are comparable to several other parts of the providers’ service area.

Therefore, WSPs are corporate public utilities with a license, given by WASREB and obtained through the WSBs, to provide water and sewerage services within their areas of operation and collect tariffs as specified in their respective Service Provision Agreement (SPA).

Although the tariff varies within the country according to different WSPs, under the human rights’ principles an affordable price needs to be charged for a minimum consumption of 20 liters per person/day. However, many users indicate that they restrict their water use because of cost. This may be partly due to incremental tariffs that punish people who share a connection (Bellaubi & Visscher, 2014).
In Ghana, no contract existed with customers; there was only a registration form for the request for connection and monthly billing against a meter reading.

Data collection comprised formal interviews and informal discussions with different public officials and senior utility staff members as well as technicians. Information was cross-checked with users, informal providers, community members and associations, staff from development agencies as well as non-governmental organizations

When comparing the results of the WSDA by different providers in Kenya, it becomes evident that all the providers had limitations but also that KIWASCO was faring better than the others, especially on quality of water and coverage. Users in Migosi seemed to limit the quantity due to cost and for MOWASCO the quantity was below the minimum needs. The two case studies in Ghana showed similar results concerning coverage and intermittent water supply. Affordability and consumption remained low in both areas.

criterion_notes.c1: Examines urban household/community water service delivery (WSD) across five case study neighbourhoods in Kenya and Ghana, including piped water supply coverage, continuity, quantity consumed, and affordability.
criterion_notes.c2: Satisfies both readings. Under the plain wording, the study examines legal, regulatory, institutional, and governance reforms in urban water service delivery in Kenya (Water Act 2002, WASREB, corporatized municipal WSPs) and Ghana (PURC, GWCL, private management contract with AVRL), alongside transparency, accountability, and participation (TAP) governance integrity and principal-agent power asymmetries. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading, it directly examines utility ownership and regulatory structures governing service provision (corporatization vs. private management contracting, licensing, and regulator oversight/sanctions), tariff and cost-recovery rules (incremental block tariffs penalizing shared connections, flat-rate billing for unmetered households, unregulated secondary provider charges), and customer contract/registration and sanction enforcement rules (one-sided billing enforcement and disconnection authority vs. unredressed utility non-supply).
criterion_notes.c3: Empirical comparative multiple-case study of five urban water service areas (three in Kenya, two in Ghana) conducted under the TISDA research program, drawing on formal interviews, informal discussions, utility/regulatory documents, participatory TAP integrity and power-asymmetry scoring, and area-based WSDA performance indicators.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports area-level service access outcomes in Table 6 and accompanying text across all five case study locations: piped water coverage (% population with piped supply as main water source), continuity (uninterrupted hours of supply per day), affordability (% of users restricting water consumption due to cost), quantity consumed (litres per person per day), and perceived water quality.
criterion_notes.c5: Identifies the study design (comparative qualitative/participatory multiple-case study), population and units of analysis (medium-to-high density low- and middle-income urban neighbourhoods, water utilities, regulators, ministries, and user-provider principal-agent dyads in Mombasa, Kisumu, Nairobi, and Accra; exact interview/household counts are not reported in this article), rule-type institutional/regulatory/tariff exposures, and service access outcomes.

study_design: Comparative qualitative and participatory multiple-case study (five urban neighbourhood/utility case studies across two countries)
population_and_sample: Five medium-to-high density, low- and middle-income urban service areas and their utilities/governance actors in Kenya (Old Town/MOWASCO in Mombasa, Migosi/KIWASCO in Kisumu, Kangemi/NCWSC in Nairobi) and Ghana (Madina and Nima/GWCL-AVRL in Accra), including public officials, regulators, utility managers and technicians, informal providers, NGOs, and water users (exact respondent sample sizes not reported).
exposure: Post-reform water sector institutional, ownership, regulatory, tariff, and contractual governance rules: corporatized municipality-owned WSPs licensed by WASREB under Kenya's Water Act 2002 vs. state-owned GWCL contracting private operator AVRL regulated by PURC in Ghana; cost-recovery, incremental block, and flat-rate tariff rules; customer agreements/registration and sanction enforcement; and principal-agent rule integrity (TAP scores) and power asymmetries.
outcome: Area-level urban water service delivery (WSDA) performance scores across five case study neighbourhoods (piped water coverage, daily hours of supply continuity, affordability measured as consumption restriction due to cost, per-capita water quantity consumed, and perceived water quality), along with institutional corruption risks and management practices.
rationale: This empirical comparative multiple-case study examines five urban water service delivery areas in Kenya and Ghana under the TISDA program. It satisfies all systematic review inclusion criteria: it examines urban household/community water service access (c1); analyzes concrete rule-type legal, regulatory, ownership, contractual, enforcement, and tariff mechanisms governing service delivery under both the plain and narrow 2026-10-13 readings of criterion 2 (c2); relies on primary qualitative interviews, document review, participatory TAP rule-integrity and power-asymmetry scoring, and area-level WSDA assessments (c3); reports empirical outcomes for piped water coverage, supply continuity, affordability/consumption restriction due to cost, and per-capita quantity (c4); clearly identifies population, unit of analysis, exposure, outcome, and case-study design (c5); and is written in English (c6). Lack of pooled quantitative effect estimates is a synthesis gate (Criterion 6), not a review-inclusion gate.
